ego.name: Vannevar Bush
ego.summary: Vannevar Bush was an American engineer, inventor, and science administrator. He developed analog computers, proposed the memex, and directed much of the United States’ wartime scientific research through the Office of Scientific Research and Development. After the war, he pressed for sustained federal support of basic science.

connections.relationship_description: Richard Perry Bush was Bush’s father and the Universalist pastor in Everett, Massachusetts. Like his son, he attended Tufts College.
connections.notes: Bush was named after John Vannevar, an old friend of his father.

connections.relationship_description: Bush's mother raised him in the Bush family household in Everett and later Chelsea, Massachusetts.
connections.notes: She was the daughter of a prominent Provincetown family.

connections.relationship_description: Bush and Phoebe Clara Davis both came from Chelsea, Massachusetts. They married in August 1916 and had two sons.
connections.notes: Their marriage lasted until her death in 1969, and they had two sons.

connections.relationship_description: Richard Davis Bush was one of Bush's two sons with Phoebe Clara Davis.
John Hathaway Bush was one of Bush's two sons with Phoebe Clara Davis.
Hazen proposed extending Herbert R. Stewart’s integraph work to second-order differential equations. Bush supervised Hazen during work on the differential analyzer from 1927 to 1931.
connections.notes: Their machine became the first widely practical general-purpose differential analyzer.

connections.relationship_description: Shannon worked as a research assistant on Bush's differential analyzer at MIT and developed his landmark 1937 master's thesis applying Boolean algebra to relay and switching circuits.
connections.notes: Bush also suggested that Shannon conduct doctoral work on mathematical genetics at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory.

connections.relationship_description: Marshall backed Bush's commercialization work, partnered with him in the Spencer Thermostat Company, and joined him in founding the American Appliance Company, later Raytheon.
connections.notes: Their 1924 work with Charles G. Smith commercialized the S-tube voltage regulator.

connections.relationship_description: Roosevelt approved Bush's proposal for the National Defense Research Committee in June 1940 and later relied on Bush's wartime science administration through the OSRD.
connections.notes: Roosevelt approved Bush’s National Defense Research Committee proposal in 1940 and appointed him director of the OSRD in 1941. Bush delivered Science, The Endless Frontier to President Harry S. Truman in 1945.

connections.relationship_description: Conant served with Bush on the NDRC, succeeded him as its chairman after the OSRD's creation, and remained a senior partner in wartime research and Manhattan Project governance.
connections.notes: Bush was Conant's alternate on the Military Policy Committee overseeing the Manhattan Project.

connections.relationship_description: Bush appointed Loomis to the NDRC, where Loomis chaired the Microwave Committee and helped establish the MIT Radiation Laboratory for radar development.
connections.notes: Their collaboration connected private scientific resources, MIT research, and the federal wartime research system.

connections.relationship_description: Kennelly was Bush's MIT doctoral adviser in electrical engineering in 1916; they clashed when Kennelly demanded additional thesis work that Bush declined to do.
connections.notes: The department chairman overruled Kennelly, allowing Bush to receive the joint MIT-Harvard doctorate.

connections.relationship_description: Bush worked under Jackson after joining MIT's Department of Electrical Engineering in 1919.
Bush and fellow MIT professor Timbie coauthored Principles of Electrical Engineering in 1922.
Stewart was Bush's master's student and, at Bush's suggestion, built an integraph in 1925 that helped lead to the differential analyzer.
Wiener guided Bush through mathematical difficulties and wrote an appendix for Bush's 1929 textbook Operational Circuit Analysis.
connections.notes: Bush described their relationship as an unusually enjoyable collaboration between an engineer and a mathematician.

connections.relationship_description: Terman earned an ScD in electrical engineering from MIT in 1924 under Bush's supervision.
connections.notes: Terman later became a major academic administrator and an important figure in the development of Silicon Valley.

connections.relationship_description: Power, owner of AMRAD, hired Bush in 1916 to run the company's laboratory while Bush was teaching at Tufts.
connections.notes: The laboratory position paid Bush more than his Tufts salary.

connections.relationship_description: Bush sought to commercialize Spencer's thermostatic-switch invention after AMRAD management declined to pursue it.
connections.notes: The resulting Spencer Thermostat Company helped establish Bush's financial independence.

connections.relationship_description: Aldrich provided backing with Marshall for the Spencer Thermostat Company, for which Bush served as consultant.
Bush, Marshall, and Smith redirected the American Appliance Company toward marketing Smith's S-tube voltage regulator for radios.
connections.notes: The company was renamed the Raytheon Company.

connections.relationship_description: Jewett was among the scientists and administrators whom Bush assembled for the National Defense Research Committee in 1940.
Tolman was a member of the National Defense Research Committee organized under Bush's chairmanship in 1940.
Rear Admiral Bowen served among the military and scientific representatives brought into the National Defense Research Committee under Bush in 1940.
Brigadier General Strong was among the Army representatives who worked with Bush through the National Defense Research Committee beginning in 1940.

category_summaries.summary: Bush grew up in Everett in a household shaped by Richard Perry Bush’s Universalist ministry and the family’s connection to Tufts College. In 1916 he married Phoebe Clara Davis, whom he had known in Chelsea. They raised two sons while Bush’s academic, industrial, and public work expanded.

MIT was the setting for Bush’s faculty career, engineering work, and technical collaborations. Arthur Edwin Kennelly supervised his doctoral work, and Dugald C. Jackson led the department Bush joined in 1919. Bush worked with William H. Timbie and Norbert Wiener and supervised students including Herbert R. Stewart, Harold Hazen, Claude Shannon, and Frederick Terman. Stewart and Hazen contributed to the work that produced the differential analyzer.

Bush’s industrial work began with AMRAD, where Harold Power hired him to run a laboratory while he taught at Tufts. Al Spencer, Laurence K. Marshall, Richard S. Aldrich, and Charles G. Smith connected him to thermostat and radio-device ventures. American Appliance Company marketed Smith’s S-tube voltage regulator and later became Raytheon.

During World War II, Bush assembled scientists, industrial researchers, and military representatives for federal defense research. Roosevelt approved the NDRC in 1940 and appointed Bush to direct the OSRD in 1941. Conant, Loomis, Jewett, Tolman, Bowen, and Strong worked in the network that connected universities, industry, and military services to wartime research.
